cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-lamb-four-.summary: In a medallion at the top, labelled 'Agnus', the Lamb with a cross-nimbus stands holding a cross-staff, while the four living creatures summon in turn the four horsemen, who ride across the coloured bands of the page below: the archer on a white horse, the rider with a sword, the rider with scales, and Death. The Lamb is shown as the one who opens the seals.
facts: With 184 surviving miniatures on 284 leaves, it is described as one of the most richly decorated and best documented of the Beatus commentaries.

The Girona Beatus was completed on 6 July 975 for an abbot Dominicus, probably at the monastery of Tábara; unusually, its painters are named: 'Ende, woman painter and servant of God', and the monk-priest Emeterius.
cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-lamb-four-.notes: The Commons title ('Jesus and the Apostles looking down on the Earth') does not describe the image; the subject is the opening of the first four seals. Christ appears as the Lamb. Folio not given.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Within a purple medallion, the haloed Christ stands holding a cross-staff, while a dark demon with a spear lurks outside at the left and arrows fly through the air at the right. The verses below speak of 'the arrow that flieth by day … the destruction that wasteth at noonday'.
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

vam:O14726.summary: The veiled Virgin sits at the centre of this bronze relief, gazing down at the dead body of her Son stretched across her knees; her right hand supports his shoulder and her left rests on his waist. Christ's head falls back, his long hair hanging loose, while two small winged angels stand on clouds at either side with their hands joined in prayer. The tender, sorrowful image once formed the door of a tabernacle, guarding the reserved Sacrament behind the figure of Christ's sacrificed body.
facts: The relief was formerly attributed to the Paduan sculptor Giovanni Minelli, but is now thought to have been made at Ferrara; its style and figure types relate closely to works in the circle of Niccolò Baroncelli (d. 1453).
It is cast in bronze in low relief, with traces of gilding, and measures about 56 by 49 cm (V&A).
vam:O14726.notes: Worklist year (850) was an error: this is a 15th-century Italian work (V&A: Ferrara, third quarter of the 15th century), so it moves out of the 1st–10th-century batch. Acquired in London (inv. 5469-1859).
